review:
This game is arguably THE best game in the Paradox library, by a large margin in my opinion, if only for the fact that you don't get to play as generic "France" bit you actually get to play as the count of Paris, and scheme your way up to becoming the emporer of the entire Holy Roman Empire.

Considering the game was free, I'll just try to advise on which DLC are worth your time to pick up. I'll go in order of best/most features to smallest.

Holy Fury: Quite a few features from The Old Gods are rolled in, except for the start date. A large expansion for pagan realms, as well as Catholicism, including coronation for Kings and Emporers, with negative consequences for not being crowned. Pagans get warrior lodges, and the choice to fine tune their reformed religion. Some features are tied to other DLC however. Includes shattered/random map generation.

Way of Life: This DLC allows your character to choose a specific "focus" for a period of time, no less than 10 years, from shagging all the ladies, to focusing on becoming the worlds greatest commander, to fratenizing with merchants. It offers a ton of features and fun events to mess with.

Conclave: Changes the way some of the core game mechanics work. Notably, changing the way the councilors work, so they can have a say in the affairs of your realm. Some people despise this DLC because it admittedly makes the game much harder to handle. For me that's a good thing. Conclave also changed the way educating children worked, from more or less copying the traits of the educator to allowing you to choose a childhood focus for them which somewhat more randomly, but organically grows the traits of the child.

Reapers Due: You can't have a Miedeval game without the Plauge, right? This DLC massively expands on the way your character can die horribly, from the usual diseases, to changing the generic "maiming" to actually losing limbs in battle, or other events.

The Old Gods: Allows you to play as a "pagan" including the Norse Vikings, to plunder the rest of the world. This DLC is highly focused around the Norse and less so around the surrounding religions. It is a solid DLC however, and it does include an earlier start date than the 1066 date.

Charlemagne: Adds the story of the Karlings, a largely scripted series of events based around the creators of "Frankia" and the creation of the Holy Roman Empire (you can quite easily change history and ruin the scripted events (in a good way) if you want though). Includes a start date even earlier than the Viking age. The story is only relavent to the player if you play as either of the Karling brothers, or the king of Lombardy (Italy), otherwise, no events will fire for the player, unless the AI makes the Empire.

Legacy Of Rome: Adds flavor to the Byzantine Empire, and any characters within it. This DLC also introduced standing armies, called "retinues", which are permanent (semi)profesional armies on the map. This is a good DLC to get, even if you have 0 interest in the Anatolia area of Europe.

Jade Dragon/Rajas of India/Sword Of Islam/Sons Of Abraham: I tie these 4 DLC together, primarially because they allow you to play a non Europe centric group of characters and religions. 

Jade Dragon allows you to play in the Tibet area of the map, and allows you to communicate with the Chinese, for boons, or banes, depending on how you treat them. This opens up the ability to play a Buhdist or Bön character, with a special government type allowing the ruler to hold temples without penalty.

Rajas of India i'm least farmiliar with, even after a few thousand hours of this game offline. I personally only have ever played in India once. However, it is an expansive DLC. Opens up Hindu and Jainisim.

Sword of Islam allows you to play as the variety of Muslim rulers across Africa, and Asia. Playing as a particularly powerful Muslim ruler can get extremely hard to manage, due to Decadence. Decadence ticks up over time as a result of particurlary impious family members, and once it reaches a certain point, it can become a full blown civil war. 

Sons of Abraham: Implemented Holy Orders (Such as the Teutonic Order, Knights Templar for example) and also allows you to play as Jewish characters.

Horse Lords/The Republic: Both of these are tied together because they allow you to play entirely different government types.

Horse Lords has the most resembelance to EU4, due to the fact that you don't get to have a "levy" of troops, but instead a "horde" (standing army of pure cavalry). The government is also revolved around having empty lands for your horses to graze upon, which also means that when you successfully invade a "civilized" peoples land, you get to raze and pillage their cities, temples, and castles to the ground to make way for more grazing land. It's a very fun way to play, but it can also get very volatile internally should clans declare feuds against each other. 

The Republic is the complete opposite. Instead of razing settlements, the nations you can play as in The Republic (notably Venice, and Genoa) revolve around building trade posts in lands bordering the coasts. These republics as a result tend to be extremely wealthy to offset the fact that in general, their armies are relatively weak. This DLC is also incredibly hard coded, and hard to work with, in some cases outright randomly giving you a game over, for no discernable reason. It's a decent DLC, but highly optional, in my opinion.

Monks and Mystics: This DLC is interesting, if only for the fact that Devil Worshipers were added with it. Most Christian nations have, more open, less nefarious societies, such as the Benidictine monastic order which your character can patronize. These orders give a variety of bonuses to your character and anyone they interact with. There's the Hermetics, basically philosiphers and wizzards, which can be very fun to play in if your character is smart enough (learning above 10) and not a tribal ruler. Then, there's the Assasins, a religious order, specializing in... well... asasinations. They're locked specifically to Shia true followers, but all characters who are not pagan can secretly convert to Shia as a result of showing interest in the society. Lastly, there's the (insert diety of evil here) worshipers. These characters get some extremely powerful clandestine actions they can preform, mostly including abduction of other characters TO START, going all the way up to performing miracles, such as regrowing limbs with some luck. Unfortunately, most non christian/muslim/eastern religions only have Devil Worshipers available to them as a society, so they are fairly common in pagan lands.

Sunset Invasion: A very ahistorical DLC, obviously. I'd personally avoid this one, mostly because it's pretty broken, and not fun to deal with. Think of a west coast Mongol invasion of Europe. At some point in your game, if you enable the features of this DLC, the Aztecs will invade Europe, with no joke, millions of men, who will stay there for hundreds of years.

[b]Optional DLC[/b]
[u]This DLC is COSMETIC ONLY.[/u]

Ultimate Unit Pack: It adds a variety of historically correct looking units to represent your armies as they move about the fields.

Ultimate Portrait Pack: Adds a ton of portraits for rulers of various cultures. I'd personally advise picking it up if you can. It feels weird sometimes having a West African character look exactly the same as a Bedouin character (not trying to be racist, but north/central africans are different peoples).

Dynasty Shield Pack: Contains a lot of historically accurate dynastic shields, such as the proper Arabic written onto the shield of the shields of most Muslim rulers, instead of a blank colored shield. Optional, but a nice addition.

Ultimate Music Collection: What it says on the tin. All of the music in the pack is amazing. I never knew I could like Metal until I bought Full Plate Metal and heard "We're that perfect storm" just as the pope called a crusade.

So I think it's about that time when I actually review this game. I've played it off steam for more than 300 hours and about 1500 hours on steam, so it's fair to say I've experienced just about all the bugs, highs and lows, DLCs' and changes to the game's mechanics through the never-ending patches on Paradox' end. 

I will preface this by saying I'm a history nerd and a complete and utter sucker for the medieval era. I'm a nostalgic dreamer who always used to dream about a game that was dynasty (family) focused, as opposed to the total warfare/dominate the universe-type game. So when I got this game as a gift, it was like someone had created the game for me. It's my go to when I just want to pass time and see whatever my Swedish countess or Scottish duke are up to. 

The level of micromanagement is ridiculous. I love it. But it's borderline insane. Go through the tutorials of the game, and you'll find yourself lost with a sensation of you might know what you did wrong. Don't go through the tutorials, and you might as well be trying to fill in for Slash at a concert, when the most experience you've had playing a guitar was looking at a banjo through a shop's window. It's intense. In the beginning I lost whole countries to distant relatives in other countries and was scratching my head, but eventually I got the hang of it. I think everyone can play this game, but you have to be prepared to put in a lot of effort and willingness to learn its mechanics. And then after that, there are lesser things to learn, such as your wife trying to kill you because you had a sweet dalliance with her sister. Or perhaps the fact that leading your own troops could result in the unfortunate event of you losing your life, and your 3-year old, imbecilic son inheriting your entire kingdom. There's always more to learn, no matter how much you play this game - its excitement will last you a long time. 

I love this game because of its neverending possibility for replayability. No game will ever be the same. You can customize your characters with an inexpensive DLC (get the DLCs - at least "The old Gods" and a few more. They add so much to the game), and you can create the basis of your new game with a new objective. 

The word sandbox is key, because in this world, you are not only the lord of your demesne, but of your own fate. Do you want to take that neighbouring county? Or do you just want to keep your family strong and safe, provide good husbands for your daughters? Maybe your king has been getting on your nerves and you want to gather allies and usurp his throne? This medieval world is all yours - if you have the gold, skill and time. 

On the downside of things, I think CK2 is worth €40, but for a four-year old game it's on the steeper side. It's frequently on sale though. Add it to your wishlist and wait; you can snatch it up for a fraction of its original price. 

I've enjoyed this game so much and had so many angry, funny and downright amazing moments. Wars I thought I'd lose have turned and I've won entire kingdoms. I've romanced my way through entire courts to get women to join my plots to kill people. The level of intrigue, surprises, horrors, joys and entertaining moments are endless. 

Oh, and...I seduced the pope once. As a gay king. 10/10.

Alright, let me spit some real game at you here. I play Crusader Kings 2 currently, I have a blast while doing so, and I have all 68 downloadable content packs for this game, acquired over the handful of years since I bought it. At the time I wrote this, I have 2,005 hours in this game, if that adds an iota of legitimacy to what I have to say here. This review isn't negative because of CK2, and I'm not bitter about the CK2 subscription model from a "I should have waited because then I would have saved money" point of view. This review is negative because of the disturbing pattern that I've noticed and thought about regarding all of Paradox Development Studio's current "grand strategy" titles (CK3, EU4, Stellaris, HOI, Imperator). This is just my perspective, and I know I will find many enemies amongst those who drank PDX's kool-aid, but I believe that what I have to say here is right and true, and all I ask is that you consider this before buying, if for nothing more than for hearing a well-informed critical perspective from the inside.

You, potential player, will find that Crusader Kings 2 seems to have a high financial barrier to entry. At the time I write this, the core, gameplay-affecting expansions cost [b]~$183 minus a 10% bundle discount[/b]. The full, [b][i]*developer-intended*[/i][/b] experience, including everything made for the game (including 2 e-books and the completely self-contained Sunset Invasion DLC), is [b]~$317 minus a 17% discount[/b]. Those price points are somewhat ludicrous, but this game is the kind I’ll still be playing 10-20 years from now. As one of those grand strategy games whose gameplay partially exists in your mind, it has the potential for that sort of soft longevity if that’s your thing.

Now, let me tell you my real beef, which is with PDX’s remarkable history of releasing DLCs that can range from competent, significant additions to unpolished or unfinished to just straight broken. Make no mistake: PDX is capable of releasing DLCs that at least seemed like it’s quality was assured by playtesters, and [b]not all DLCs come out in a bad state[/b], but any fellow CK2-heads will recall [u]Way of Life[/u]’s release (every AI took the seduction focus, so the whole world had herpes and syphilis) and [u]Conclave[/u]’s release (The threat system was unbalanced to the point where an Irish duke taking a single county would result in the Pope and the Caliph banding together to take you down a peg. The council was so overpowered that one funny review said something like [i]“tl;dr: paradox thinks there were constitutional elective monarchies in the 8th century”[/i]). Let’s not forget EU4’s [u]Common Sense[/u] and its patch (gave the AI the ability to develop provinces, but not the player unless you bought the DLC; only recently rectified), and what appears to be the case with Stellaris’s [u]Overlord[/u] (haven’t bought it, but the reviews detail a similar experience on launch of a clearly untested DLC that introduces bugs and design issues). All that is to say that there is definitely a lack of QA testing done by PDX for their DLCs. On the one hand, this makes sense. The people who made this game are in their 30s and 40s and 50s with families, kids, and mortgages. They don’t have time to play a video game for long enough to provide adequate QA suggestions, and PDX (or any company that controls a game as a service) will not pay for the QA testing required to ensure a good product because (1) their games get too big, ergo (2) to properly QA test everything to ensure a well-made product would require a robust QA department and an amount of money and time on their end that they are unwilling to spend. That would eat into the bottom line for no other purpose than to make a better game, which isn’t [i]necessarily[/i] profitable. I think you’ll find that PDX grand strategy DLCs and their accompanying patches mirror strongly the patches of League of Legends in both execution and outcome: Changes will be introduced to a game by people who don’t play said game, resulting in changes that don’t accurately reflect what the game needs to be healthy or complete, leading to the frustration of players on the ground and a loss of goodwill from cynics like me. This is the natural sacrifice of a game as a service, and you need to realize this before buying into CK2, whether monthly or wholesale: CK2 and all extant PDX grand strategy games are services whose cost for full ownership of the [b][i]*developer-intended*[/i][/b] experience is obscenely high.

I was there for Stellaris on launch day. I even pre-ordered it for the little bug guy portrait in-game. For those who can recall, 1.0 Stellaris, from a design perspective, is unrecognizable from what we have today. There are so many added and removed systems in current Stellaris that weren’t even considered before its release. This makes me question “Why?” Why would they release a game only to so radically change it down the line? Wouldn’t they have been better off taking a few years and just making one finished game? This can be a matter of perspective, though. Where some people see that and say “Well, PDX needs money to continue the development of the game,” I see that and say “I paid for a game, not a service, so I expect a complete product for my $40-$60, not a perfectly breakable platform to sell me further products.” My problem with all the PDX Dev Studio DLCs isn’t that I don’t like extra stuff being made for a game I like. It’s that there are certain features baked into the CK2 DLCs (excluding Sunset Invasion) that are arguably essential, even if some consider them to just be nice-to-haves. For instance, the Old Gods DLC is fantastic, thematic, and absolutely essential. The component I think is most essential to the DLC and ought to have been baked into the game to begin with was the pushing back of the start date from 1066 (this was way before the free Iron Century update) to 867. To me, the pushing back of the start date is literally more game that is added by just adjusting a couple of values and looking at some real life maps for reference. The analogy I came up with is that this part of Old Gods DLC and those like it (i.e., those DLCs containing non-relevant features that affect the core gameplay) are like the back door to a house you buy. Sure, the back door isn’t strictly necessary for the house to be a house, but having to specifically pay extra for it on top of the house itself is kinda sus. Why wasn’t a back door specified in the original design for the house?

In the end, I can’t recommend CK2. I can’t recommend it in good faith without informing you of the DLC practices of the company that made it. If you in the future choose to buy a PDX Development Studio grand strategy game, you should be prepared for that game to meet one of three fates: either it becomes bloated beyond belief (EU4), it becomes a complete product after almost a decade (CK2), or it will be shelved indefinitely in a somewhat polished yet undercooked and barren state (Imperator: Rome). 

TL;DR: The PDX Grand Strategy model enables the release of sub-standard games and DLCs, and you paying $5 a month (or God forbid $317) for the [b][i]*developer-intended*[/i][/b] CK2 experience after the highs and lows it has been through is an endorsement of that release practice, which I don’t think you should do. If you buy any other PDX Dev Studio title on launch day, just know you are buying into a service, not a complete game.

My friend and I decided to play a multiplayer game of Crusader Kings II earlier. Never in my life have I ever been more frightened in a video game. Let me explain.

My friend exact words were, "Your son is a demon, you have to kill him or it will be too late."

"Too late?" I asked. My friend remained silent. At the time, the only way to kill your own child was to imprision them and execute them. So, I decided I would try to do that. Well, whenever I tried to imprison "Forgot the Condom", he ended up escaping and fleeing the country. I explain this to my friend and he tells me, "We have to kill him, somehow." At the time, neither my friend nor I knew about the character search tool in the game, so we had to manually find "Forgot the Condom" in all of the provinces. We looked for 30 minutes, and could not find him. After we finished searching, we decided to continue with the game as normal. "Let's just hope nothing bad happens", my friend exclaimed.

Five years pass, and I get a notification. It reads: "My dear daughter 'SWAGYOLO420NOSCOPE" must have suffered a stroke in her sleep last night. She was found drooling in bed, one eye bloodshot, mumbling about a small monster that stabbed her in the eye before it ran off. There are dark rumours about the so called 'demon child', my son 'Forgot the Condom', again... As always when something terrible happens, she does seem inordinately happy." I thought we had been rid of "Forgot the Condom", but he was back, with a vengeance.

I tried finding "Forgot the Condom" again in all of the provinces near me, but I could not find him.

Another year passes, my son "URLUCKYIDIDNTABORTU" dies. Then my daughter, "6 Salads" dies. My son, "Taco Tuesday" dies. At this point I realized, "Forgot the Condom" is killing all of my children. I entirely dedicated to finding and killing him. I'm looking around for him, and he is killing all of my children. We look for him for 2 years in game, when my friend says something.

"HOLY SHIT, I FOUND HIM!"

"WHAT WHAT, WHERE IS HE?" I ask.

"Holy shit, he.... he"

"What? What's wrong?"

"He is the FUCKING POPE."

I immediately check to see if he is right. My son... my son, "Forgot the Condom" is the fucking Pope. 

My friend and I start to freak out, "How the hell did he become the Pope?!?!" "What do we do?" "HOW DID WE NOT NOTICE THIS BEFORE?!?!?!"

Immediately we start a plot to kill "Forgot the Condom". We have to kill him before it's too late. We have to kill him before it's too late. We have to kill him before it's too late.

We had 167% plot power, we were going to kill him, but then the worst thing happen. I get a notification: "My dear son 'Ebola Paitent 0' has died." So, what is so special about Ebola Paitent 0? Well, Ebola Paitent 0 was the Emperor of the Holy Roman Empire, aka my friend. My demon child "Forgot the Condom" killed my friend. At this point in the game, the entirety of my children and lineage, the ISIS family line, had been completely wiped out. Except for one person, except for me, "12, 12 of the family ISIS". I could no longer kill my son because you cannot plot against your children, I was stuck. I had no where to go. I was going to die, the ISIS family line was going to die. 

I struggled to find any way to kill the Pope, my friend could not start a plot because his new character was a child. We had nowhere to turn. We were out of options.

Eventually, the worst came, "Forgot the Condom" killed me in my sleep. I was dead, the legendary "12 of ISIS" was dead.

The game ended. I had no heirs, and I was eliminated from the game. The game was also hosted by me so it ended for my friend as well.

"WHAT THE FUCK was that?" my friend said. I didn't even say anything. A few minutes pass, we were staring at the defeat screen the entire time.

"We must remember this in some way." I explained. "We must remember '12 of ISIS' and 'Forgot the Condom'. We need to memoralize them forever." "How do we do that?" my friend asks.

"I don't know, but we must remember them. They are legends and must never be forgotten."

If you care about the amount of gameplay you get for your money at all, this game probably rates higher than any other game. (Last I read, the [i]average[/i] player had over 500 hours on this game.) 

Crusader Kings II is a strategic game where you spend most of your time looking at a big map of Europe cut into little counties, but it is [i]drastically[/i] different from a game like Medieval II: Total War.  Whereas in those games, every nation had rigid boundaries and an entire nation was a distinct, unified entity, Crusader Kings II focuses upon the feudal system of governance, and especially its hereditary system of succession.

You are not a nation, you are an extended family through the ages.  You may start as King of England, but lose the throne in a succession war, only to wind up inheriting the Kingdom of France, instead.  It is a game of political machinations more than warfare.

You can't just declare war whenever you want to, you need to, by hook or by crook, manage to get a claim to that land you want to invade.  Battles are relatively quick and hands-off (play that Total War if you want to manage the troops directly) but it's the space between wars that makes the game interesting.  To get that claim, you probably need to find some way to get the princess of that land in your bed (or your son's bed), and it's this medieval bloodline plotting that make up the meat of the game.  

For that matter, you don't necessarily need to declare war to gain land - just marry into the family that succeeds a throne, and make sure that, one way or the other, your chosen heir also manages to be the chosen heir of a target kingdom, and the kingdoms will be unified upon the death of your current character and the current king of the target land. 

Likewise, just because you gain land doesn't mean you can keep it.  You need to delegate land out, and succession laws can fragment your kingdom so much that you see hard-conquered lands slip out of your grasp by inheritence without your consent.  EDIT: And since writing this, Conclave has come out to add complexities to keeping your nobles in line.

Worse, while whomever you give land will be quite grateful for the first 20 years of their rule or so, their children will have no gratitude for the gift of land your father gave them, and will likely be burning with ambitions you have to keep in check.  Every few decades, your character ages and dies, and succession wars and civil wars are the primary way the game keeps your over-arching ambitions in check.  Rather than letting a large empire mean that no external threat can challenge you, and no internal threats exist, the larger you become, the less vulnerable you are to external threats, but the more vulnerable you are to internal ones. You spend more and more time trying to find a way to bludgeon the rebellious nobles and religious minorities into line.

If you get tired of games of Total War, and don't bother completing them because, once you are the strongest power on the map, there's nothing to do but steamroll everything else that stands in your path, then CK2 is a great remedy to this.  (You can still make a world-spanning super-empire, but it's much more interesting to try to keep it when the owners of that land still fight you when you plant your flag there than to just have them mutely pay taxes to you and have assumed loyalty to your cause.)

It's a game that's just hard and realistic enough to make the things you do actually feel like you're thumbing your nose at history.  You can play an Irish earl, rise to High King of Ireland, and conquer England.  Or play as the West Africans, and conquer the Muslims and convert them to your pagan faith.  Being a norse viking that captures the pope and sacrifices him to Odin is always fun.  (And nabs the Holy Smoke! achievement.) And if you do it with an unbroken line of Viking empresses, all the better.

Mods are also a high point: Play the Elder Kings mod, based upon the Elder Scrolls, and conquer Cyrodiil and beyond as an immortal or vampire, using magicks to summong hordes of demons when under threat. There's an A Game of Thrones mod, as well, and mods to turn the game into something like a space 4X game.  

DLC still comes out for the game, as well.  While more than a little annoying to be nickled and dimed, the trickle of new content keeps the game fresh and new achievements are meaningful challenges, requiring players to take up historic underdogs to rise to glory.  Getting a full board of achievements is extraordinarily difficult, but enjoyable for the challenge they provide.  Compare this to Activision, Ubisoft, or EA, where you buy iterations of the same game every year, and throwing down $10 for another year's worth of life in a game is well worth the price.

Determined to unite Ireland. Crazy Norse wife kills all my spymasters, poisons 2 of my sons in less than a year. 

Half a year later adventurer from spain threatens me and I think "It's fine, he's no threat to me." 1 year later, 30,000 angry men attack my fledgling, petty kingdom, vassals declare independance, revolt happens and king dies from head injury in battle.

3 year old son put on the throne only to be poisoned by wife. 

10/10, would play again.

There is a reason I have sunk nearly 1,400 hours into this game, academic and professional life be damned,

This game has near infinite replay value, and although it is helpful to have an appreciation for the historical time period, it is not required given the sheer levels of zaniness that can be achieved.  Whether you approach this as a historian, a fan of Game of Thrones, or as someone who wants to be a medieval Caligula and name their horse Glitterhoof as Chancellor, it's unlikely you will be disappointed by this masterpiece of a game.

I'm not gonna lie to you, the learning curve for this game is a real biggy. And some people might look at that and decide that isn't worth their time. I thought the same a couple of years ago when I played the game when it was free for a weekend. I downloaded it and decided to play as a count in France. But I was unable to figure out how to even raise my troops, so I quit after an hour of faffing about.

A couple of years later I started watching a video series on youtube by the one and only Northernlion. I ended up only watching half of it because I wanted to give CK2 a second try now that i thought that I had learned a bit. So I bought the game, for real this time.

I started to play as a irish duke this time (to be specific, a ruler design character as the Duke of Mide at 1066 start date) and I was hooked, I couldn't stop playing. The game occupied me day and night, I only let it rest when I had to go to school, do homework, eat and sleep. I ended up quitting my Irish playthrough and starting a new. And after that a new and after that a new and so on... There was so many endless possibilities to play this game, and I wanted to play and experiencing them all. I suppose that now that I've logged over 1,000 hours playing Crusader Kings 2 I should carve out a little time to say that this is demonstrably my favorite game of all time (by a factor of five, if you're curious).  There are 16,000 other reviews that will give you more details of what's great and what's not about the game, but let me just add that I have never found a game that better simulates [i] internal [/i] political conflict within a country.  Think about it: you play most "great" strategy games like Civilization, and you'd think that nations were made up of uniform automatons - the worst it gets there is some city riots because you didn't build enough "Happiness" buildings.  

In CK2 your vassal rulers are individuals, with their individual ambitions and characteristics, and they can be a real pain to manage - sometimes they fight with one another, sometimes they fight with you, and ultimately it's about who's got the most leverage.  The only difference between CK2 politics and modern democratic politics is that "leverage" in the 12th century is usually counted in swords; besides that, the backstabbing and intriguing is pretty indistinguishable.  A strong king, just like a strong president, is one who dominates their internal foes so that they can in turn dominate their external ones.

That simple innovation is what's made this my all-time favorite game, the one I've been coming back to year after year.  Add to that a dedicated modding community that let's you play out the same internal/external conflict in Game of Thrones, Ancient Rome, or Warhammer, and, well, you've got at least a thousand hours of fun ahead of you.

With 400 hours played, my biggest hope is that they stop releasing new DLC so that I can stop buying it.

The game is certainly not for everybody, and as above the amount of DLC can be intimidating.  But if you enjoy the thought of creating a dynasty and playing it throughout history then this might be the game for you.

I've now gone back to 867ad Italy, with the Duke of Tuscany, Adelberto Bonifazi. The king of Italy, a foreign invader from the Karling Dynasty of France is leige to the 5 major Italian duchies, and is moderately respected within Italy. Europe is divided from west to east by three different Karling Kings, and the throne of Italy is up for grabs within their house. It makes for fantastic storytelling of italian unification, or fragmentation (which is more consistant with the history books). Find any dynasty that tugs at your fairytale strings and you'll create the adventure yourself. You compile your own ruleset for winning, and you'll play again and again to get it 'just right'. 

You are allowed to pick and choose from a wonderful list of histrorical characters from the 760's through the 1300's (more with DLC). You might even find yourself on wikipedia learning about how europe, northern africa and western asia used to work. Once you are briefly educated on succession laws, title claimancy, and holy war you'll be well on your way to taking Rome for the Byzantine empire and converting all Christians to Orthodox and thus resolving the great schism, or perhaps you'll begin as a small vassal, in control of a single county and have your progeny expand and reclaim The Holy Roman Empire. Or maybe you'll just want to keep a small duchy in Italy safe from foreign invasion generation after generation and keep your family safe at all costs. 

It is at its core a sandbox game. You create the goals, you amend them, the world changes drastically, your position changes, there's an opening, the window closes, alliances are broken, new friends arrive at court to save the day, and eventually you forget what the original goal of winning was to begin with. You watch and contribute to the story as generations of genetic triumphs and failures are constantly bickering, warring, dieing, plotting, changing sides for no good reason, and are also generally trying to make sure you don't have a larger army than they do. Don't forget about all the neighbors, who are convinced that they would be better suited to rule in your lands than you are.

There are a thousand pitfalls to success in CK2 as there surely were in the more noble times, so always learn from your mistakes and try again. Use google. And always have enough gold to hire an appropriately sized mercenary army and pay them for 12 months. Always. Eight hour playthroughs that fall because of premature spending will remind you of that. Keep your neighbor rulers in the character watch list, keep a constant eye on beneficial marriages, and constantly scan the character find sheet for potential courtiers that would join your court and could serve as councilmembers. Remember that the safety of the family is top priority, so always be able to defend yourself, be it through your own army, your vassals or your alliance's, but never have a substantially smaller force than the neighbors or vassals. That will always spell game over. 

And lastly, please try to remember at all times that those who cannot remember the past are doomed to repeat it.

If you'd like a review that is about the game, and not a complaint about DLC, here's mine.

A basic summation: Crusader Kings II is a grand strategy game where the player plays as a Middle Ages monarch. The overarching aim of the game is to keep your bloodline's descendants in power over something. When I say something, it might be something as small as a single county in Ireland, or it might be the entire Kingdom of England. Your line of succession is one of the most important facets of the game: as long as you have a viable heir your game will not end even on death, because you will be reassigned to play as that heir. If you ever fail to secure an heir of your bloodline, your game will end.

Which brings me to a description of the game's freeform nature: you cannot "win" this game, because there are no victory conditions. The player's goals are their own to try and achieve. What the game does have are a variety of game over conditions that should be avoided, such as being defeated in war and deposed or the aforementioned lack of an heir. As long as you avoid game over, you're free to do whatever you want in your realm and in the world. If you'd prefer to play as a humble vassal to the Holy Roman Emperor, you can do that. If you'd prefer to try and overthrow your liege via war or intrigue, you can do that. If you want to skip the trouble and simply choose to play as Holy Roman Emperor, you can do that!

That said, the game presents interesting and realistic limitations to whatever you do. As I've mentioned, family is a large part of the game. Having viable, capable heirs (not inbred or sick and well-taught with good traits) is a must and you must be careful how your holdings are distributed. Nothing feels worse than spending a character's lifetime conquering a massive dominion, only to have it split in two on his death because his two sons share the inheritance via Gavelkind succession. Speaking of conquering, a player cannot simply declare war - he must have a casus belli, or a reason to do so first. Whether that reason is a courtesan with a weak claim on some faraway land thanks to a slightly-noble birth, or holy war, or even a false claim generated via intrigue, there must be something to claim when sending troops abroad.

Another massive part of this game is dealing with reputation and other people. Your reputation, especially with your subjects, is ever-important. Your nature (and traits) and your actions both affect your standing with every person in the game. Everyone from the Pope to the Earl of Nowheresville has an opinion of you, and they matter! If you are a long-tenured, brave, just, pious monarch, your subjects by and large will admire you and very few will be significantly opposed to your rule. But if you are more cruel, arbitrary, and a bad person, many people will come to hate you. As a general rule, many people (particularly of religions other than your own) will hate you and it doesn't matter much, but it's much worse when many powerful people who desire your throne detest you. Revolutions in your land from angry subjects or ambitious vassals will leave you treading carefully.

I'll note that this game is very much like life: often very fun and interesting, but frequently difficult and punishing, with a knack for dealing a blow and then kicking you while you're down. You will have your best ruler ever die of a sudden illness at the age of 32, to be succeeded by his idiot son who himself will live to 80. You will have an opportunistic revolt while you're overseas crusading. You will have treacherous relatives and complicit rivals, and at times it will feel like the game is overwhelmingly against you, because it often is! Just remember that like in life, bad things happen, but with some perseverance all can be overcome.

If this wasn't already clear, this game is incredibly complex. The amount of actions and micromanagement possible is simply astounding. This gives the game a steep learning curve and the in-game tutorial is near useless. There are a number of very helpful YouTube tutorials which can be watched to help learn the game, and I'd recommend spending some time there before diving in. Once the game "clicks," it's easy to follow, but learning all the systems and actions is daunting without outside help. I'll say this: this game is not the sort of game a person can buy on sale and leap right into for a few hours of good fun. It's the sort of game you spend some time learning, and then gameplay becomes incredibly immersive. It takes some effort, but it is also very worth it.

I'll conclude this review by commenting on the DLC policy that has generated such revulsion in recent months. This game is 5 years old and is priced at $40 for the base with $200+ in DLC that many people will claim are necessary otherwise the game is empty or broken. My rebuttal is simple: firstly, the game is excellent and incredibly enjoyable without any DLC. I bought and played my first playthrough in the vanilla base game, and it was great! The basic experience is to play as a Catholic ruler of a European nation in 1066 or later. The DLCs add a variety of functions: start the game earlier in history (769 or 867,) and play as other religions and nations outside of Europe. Sword of Islam predictably allows one to be a Muslim, Rajas of India an Indian, and so on. DLC features are not necessary if one is not interested in what they allow. My personal thoughts on the game/its DLC for new players: this game often goes on a good sale where the base is $5 or $10 and the DLC are all around 50 percent off. During a sale, one can purchase the game and every worthwhile DLC for less than $50. Given that these sales happen frequently, it does not take very much patience to have this great game for not a lot of money.

Lastly, for reference, what I'd consider my "essential" list - these can be purchased together on sale for around 25-30 dollars total, and by themselves give an immersive and brilliant experience: 

- Base game

- Legacy of Rome: adds many interesting things for the Romans, but it's mostly for retinues which allows the player to form a standing army, very useful

- The Old Gods: allows for play as Pagans and gives the 867 start date, but importantly also makes revolts much more threatening and interesting

- Sons of Abraham: allows for play as Jews, but also includes many improvements for Catholicism and makes holy orders (Knights Templar, Hospitallers, etc.) far more interesting

- The Reaper's Due: adds the Black Plague/minor epidemics, but also entirely reworks disease and makes it much more interesting

This review is meant for any new player joining the fray of Crusader Kings but also contains some remarks about the future of the platform. Crusader Kings is a grand strategy game slash feudalism simulator focussing on dynasty mechanics and the intricacies of realm inheritance. In this simulation, thousands of feudal lords and overlords interact with each other, all with different personalities and different interests. Your goal: to make sure your dynasty survives the Middle Ages and becomes as powerful as possible. You do this by managing your vassals and your dynasty members (your main task) and waging war (your secondary task). 

Want your dynasty to control the throne of France? Murder the king of France, marry his wife (which will make you king but will not give your dynasty a right to the throne) and finally get a son with the French wench who will have a right to wield the standard of Saint Denis! You'd rather want to stay a vassal of the king of France and coerce his royal highness into strengthening your interests? That's even more enjoyable! Keep up your levy strength, get a seat on his council and murder off anyone who opposes you. This more or less is what makes the game tick and also what makes it fun. Because every dynasty member has his strength and weaknesses, you are constantly battling the odds.

To put it simply. The game is loads of fun and extremely entertaining. It will take you definitely dozens of hours to learn and appreciate the complexity of the mechanics that are working underneath the hood of this magnificent feudalism simulator, but it is worth it. Power through it! PLEASE! 

But what about the dozens of DLC that are available for this title, you might ask. Do I need them? The answer is "sort of". They make the game deeper and more enjoyable. Especially the ones that introduce more mechanics like the Early Middle Ages start, the Vikings expansion, the brotherhoods and the Way of Life mechanics.

But I would also like to make the point here that the "platform" format that Paradox Games, the developer and producer of the series, are using in almost all of their grand strategy games (CK2, EU4 and HOI4) is getting problematic. Ever more and more DLC's are piled on top of code that is getting dated and does not take advantage of new and better ways of simulation and calculation. Crusader Kings II came out in 2012. We are now almost in 2018. 

It will be very hard for both Paradox and the players of Crusader Kings to switch over to a sequel. Players have invested hundreds of euro's/dollars in the old platform and will be anxious about starting with a new "empty" Crusader title. Paradox will want to maximize profit and squeeze every penny out of the old platform for as long as it can. The longer it goes on, the harder the switch to Crusader Kings III will be.My opinion? We need a platform switch now! We need a better and quicker simulation! We need a better UI. We need to bring Crusader kings into 2018 and 2019 as quickly as possible.

Crusader Kings II is one of the most deep, fascinating and replayable strategy games I have ever played. In brief, you play as a family in the middle ages, anywhere between Mali and Mongolia, or from Bengal to Britain. You try to secure advantageous alliances and strategic marriages, and build up a small realm, either as a vassal of a greater power or striking out independently. There is no real win condition, though I love taking people who lost out historically, and helping push them to greatness.

The fundamental basics of a grand strategy are all there: control land and resources, use those to establish an army with which you assert control over more land and resources. However, Crusader Kings II offers alternate paths to power. subterfuge, marriage and diplomacy can also serve as paths to glory, beyond raw martial might. Very frequently you will find yourself alternating between these different options as the scenarios change.

What sets Crusader Kings II apart is that it is a game of characters. Your realm is not a single ruler with an army of loyal drones. You must entrust the rule of your lands to subordinate rulers and vassals, all of whom must be managed so that they provide you with troops, gold, and most important of all, loyalty. Thus, Kingdoms, Empires and Duchies, Steppe Khaganates and Mediterranean Sheikhdoms are all ephemeral things which can merge, split, grow and collapse, and they all do so as a product of the complex web of human interactions that this game simulates. Part of this is family politics: younger brothers will plot to better their position within the family, stepmothers will strive to press the advantage of their own children over those from previous marriages, and impatient heirs may chafe with their desire for your titles. Beyond this, you will struggle with your court and vassals. Some may be true and loyal friends, others can be bought off with gifts and honours, while many shall ever be ready to work against you for their own interests: greater power, privileges, and the chance to someday seize your position and rule for themselves. And every single realm on the map is subject to the same web of political intrigue. THIS is the magic of Crusader Kings II.

What this does for a strategy game cannot be understated. What Crusader Kings II creates is a game that can be enjoyably played at every level, from a lowly count ruling a single territory on the map, to an emperor whose realm would measure up alongside the greatest of historical powers. And in each different place, the game feels meaningfully different. A pagan tribal lord in the snowy north of Europe may run a realm rich in manpower, and poor in gold, prone to collapse on succession. A feudal count might scheme to build up his own power within another's realm, both to secure his own status, and to provide a base of support to further his ambitions to ever higher titles. And an independent ruler is threatened less and less by external forces, and more and more by the people who have been entrusted with power beneath her.

Because of this structure of power, Crusader Kings II does several things that make it stand out from other strategy games. The game has real, impactful setbacks that can befall even a strong and stable realm. In many other games, growth is geometric- a small early advantage will very frequently grow into a huge advantage later on. As a result of this, in other games, suffering a setback can feel like a game-ending disaster. However, in Crusader Kings, you may find your realm usurped from you due to a sudden string of misfortune, and be reduced to a terribly weakened position. But this is not the end- there always remains a genuine opportunity for recovery, because the game is playable from all positions!

I will, in the interest of criticism, address several issues that I have with the game. Multiplayer lobbies are clunky and awkward, and it can grow very tiresome to organize a group when a single player desyncing leads to every player needing to restart and reload the game, which frequently leads to ten to fifteen minute interruptions in play. The difficulty curve is also punishingly and unnecessarily steep steep. The game does not provide an updated tutorial that is anywhere near sufficient to familiarize new players with the mechanics of the game. Talking to more experienced players, watching videos, and reading third party guides is all but mandatory, and I think that Paradox could do better in this regard. Additionally, the user interface is large and not streamlined. This compounds the issues of new players who might be turned away from the game, before they're able to experience all of the things that I have praised earlier. Finally, the Paradox DLC policy may be good for funding the continued development of a base game for years, but it also builds up into an absurdly intimidating price wall, which I find to be unreasonable. Unless you are unconcerned with how much you spend on games, wait for sales.

Crusader Kings II is one of my most played games on Steam, and I see no reason why that will change in the future. It does things that no other game does, and sits in a unique position that rewards a wide variety of playstyles, and can be played as a serious strategy game, or as a roleplaying engine. While I've criticized aspects of the multiplayer experience, I cannot emphasize enough how much fun it is to play with friends, and there are myriad exciting mods if the default setting ever manages to grow old. If you know someone who plays it, it is absolutely worth picking up the base game on a sale. In multiplayer, you will be able to use the DLC of your host, which gives you an affordable way to sample all of the additional game mechanics.

[h1]Incest simulator ?[/h1]
This is the title that many jokingly have given this game on the internet. 
However this far from what the game is, can you perform incest, yes, however the deepth and dynamics goes far beyond mere incestual relations. 

[h1]Main purpose or goal?[/h1]
You are the head of a dynasty, at the beginning of the game, you can choose which dynasty, and who within that dynasty that you want to play as. 
Do you want to take control of one of the powerful rulers of the mighty Karling dynasty? 
Or do you want to repeat history by trying to bring a small count in Switzerland from an obscure family known as Habsburg to their glory, as Emperor of the Holy Roman Empire, and spread the Habsburg from there on. 

With the customize ruler DLC you expand you game a thousandth-fold, you will have to power to not only choose who you want to play as, but you can create you whole new dynasty and ruler. Want a genius hunchback who rules over the Arabian Empire? 
Do you want to try and backstab your way to the top of the Byzantine Empire with a powerful spy? 
It is up to you!

There is one indicator on how well you have done, that is your [b]Score[/b] which the game at the end compare with other great historical dynasties. You increase your score by having rulers with high prestige and piety, but also having other dynasty members in high positions, will generate prestige to your dynasty, giving newborn a higher starting position in life, when it comes to their prestige.

[h1]There are so many DLCs![/h1]
Many seem to get overwhelmed by the amount of DLCs this game has, however many of those are cosmetic DLCs, adding other graphics or sounds to the game. 

The main DLCs that expand gameplay are:

I will rank them, with the top being the most important expansion to get first, by my own opinion.

[olist]
[*]Ruler Designer - This will enable you to create your own ruler, only your imagination will limit the replayability of the game.
[*]Legacy of Rome - This expansion not only gives more deepth to the Orthodox rulers of the Byzantine, and greek cultures, it also provides new game mechanics, such as military retinues. [i](Also allow the possibility for castrating and blinding prisoners playing as a ruler of the Byzantine culture group)[/i]
[*]The Old Gods - This enable you to play the game from 867 CE, and also make Pagans and Zoroastrian rulers playable.
[*]Sword of Islam - Makes muslims playable, as The Old Gods each unique religion has its own mechanics.
[*]Sons of Abraham - Adds more deepth to the abrahamic faiths and also Judaism. Heresies for religions are also possible.
[*]The Republic - Want to try out the merchant life of Venice? With this DLC that will be possible, take control of a patrician family, amass wealth and control the trade zones around the shores of the known world.
[*]Charlemagne - Introduces a new starting time, at 769 CE, gives you the option to create custom Kingdoms and Empires.
[*]Rajas of India - Allows for control of the Indian rulers. 
[*]Way of Life - Focus the life of your ruler towards certain areas of his life, want to became a great hunter to catch the fable white bear? Or became the greatest architech in the whole realm?
[*]Customization Pack - Customize your ruler ingame, change the beard, hair style, even the dynasty name or shield.
[*]Sunset Invasion - If you want to add an extra level of crazy to your game, only recommended for veteran players of CK2, what if the Aztec discovered Europe first? And decided to invade?
[*]Save Game converter - If you own Europa Universalis IV and want to continue your saga from CK2, this DLC will enable you to export your CK2 game into EU IV.
[/olist]

All the other DLCs are cosmetical.

[h1]Mods![/h1]

Crusader Kings 2 has more mods, that will expand your game, one of the more popular mods is a total conversion into a Game of Thrones universe. Where you can encounter spoilers from the series, but it will also make you play out the stories in George R.R. Martin's universe in another direction, should Tyrion Lannister have the Iron Throne? 

[h1]Learning curve?[/h1]
It has a steep learning curve, and the ingame tutorial only scratches the surface of possibilities. I would recommend picking up the game, and play with a friend online, or experiment as a count in Ireland. 

But when you get a hang on it, it will grab you, and pull you deeper into a world of intrigue, murder, war, romance, and much more. In an forever going struggle for power over the realm, and the world.

UPDATE: After a whole string of expansions came out since originally writing this review in Feb 2012, I've decided to re-write it and have added in the list below, containing some of the more essential expansions, as not all are necessarily required:

LEGACY OF ROME - This pack adds retinues and factions. As I recall it originally got a bad rap as it didn't unlock additional regions of the map to the player (like Sword of Islam, for example), but these days it really is a staple expansion, and adds a lot to the game.
THE OLD GODS - Vikings! And an early start date. Honestly, I feel that the Norse add enough that this is worth putting on the 'essentials' list, as it does shake things up a bit, from the standard 'European feudal lord' formula. Might want to get this after playing a game or two of CK2 though, as a regular feudal lord, perhaps.
WAY OF LIFE - I might get flak from some people by putting this into the 'essential' list, but it adds a lot more to do, during peace time. Plus Paradox has fixed the Europe-wide orgy caused by the 'seduction' focus being super-powerful, so it's not as crazy as it was right after its initial release. (For better or for worse! :P )

And now for a "good to have, but maybe don't get it until you've played the game a few times" list. (Rolls right off the tongue, eh?)

SONS OF ABRAHAM - Adds more options, events, etc. for the three Abrahamic faiths (Christianity, Judaism and Islam). Solid expansion, but not strictly required. Good for a second playthrough, or if it's on-sale when you first buy/play the game.
CONCLAVE - Kind of goes hand-in-hand with WoL above, I feel. Adds more to do (particularly during peacetime) as you're not the sole power within your realm, as your council will try and gradually curb your power and become a force to be reckoned with - so don't underestimate your councilors! Definitely adds a fair bit more difficulty though, as this expansion can result in a lot more civil wars occurring, if you aren't adept at ingame diplomacy and gaining favours, etc. so you may want to save this for your second playthrough.
SWORD OF ISLAM - Makes Muslim rulers playable, and adds in decadence mechanics for them. Good for a second or third playthrough, after you have your fill of playing as a Christian.
THE REPUBLIC - Same as SoI above, except it makes Republics playable. Adds in trading post mechanics (among others) for more money-making opportunities.
REAPER'S DUE - This pack expands upon the existing disease mechanics, and makes the Black Death a very real threat! It also allows you to hire a court physician, who will then proceed to cut your leg off and/or gouge your eye out, in order to cure your cold. Fun expansion, but not essential.
CHARLEMAGNE - This adds in a start date even earlier than TOG's start. Good if you want extremely long games that wind up taking a heavily alt-history route, but be aware that Europe will most likely be occupied by 4-5 huge blobs by 1066, so it might become a bit of a slog, late-game.
RAJAS OF INDIA - OK if you want to play in India, but be warned that unless you get a huge, sprawling empire going, there won't actually be much (if at all) interaction between India and the rest of the game world. Really, I think they could've just made this into a separate game mode/campaign option.

Wanna make your loyal little brother an anti-pope since the pope excommuniated you because the french king (who happens to be his best friend) really hate you? Wanna make your last born son your heir even though he has 6 older brothers because he has by far the best stats since he was born a genius. Problems ? The usual with any Paradox game, DLC, DLC,DLC. A fair bit of the DLCs add a lot of great and new fun content, I'd say all of em' do its just it's gonna hit your wallet decently if you wish to get them all and it's rather scummy that basic things suchs as changing your current ruler's haircut is a 5 euro DLC. Granted, that's the worst case, there's quiet a bit of DLCs that are more fairly priced and offer some amazing content such as the Reaper's Due and a Way Of Life.
You do have to pick a few of them up or the game will feel a bit barron and underwhelming with things to do, so here's my list of some of the really necessary essential DLCs, which i will always note for any Paradox Game, only buy them in sales or if you're a crippling addicted to them, you'll most likely buy them without sales at some point in the future and then feel a bit depressed when you look at your bank account.

Necessary Essential DLCs :
1 : A Way Of Life - [ Adds a TON of new events to the game and adds focuses for characters to pick which add special abbilaties such as seduction,going out to party,hunting or personally spying on people which makes the game a lot more alive and fun, if you had to pick only one, this is the one you simply need to have to play the game as it adds so much more to the fun roleplaying aspect]

2: The Reaper's Due - [ Adds a Plague mechanic to the game , see horrible diseases spread through the world and do your best to combat them by building hospitals, getting a good healer in your court to take care of your family, adds a lot of new worryingly amazingly made deaths sounds when someone dies from the many flavors of death the game provides with this dlc which are not all just based on diseases but also executions and what not. It even adds a special execution screen where you can do mass executions at the same time, it's great]

4: Monks and Mystics - [ This DLC adds socities to the game that add a lot to the roleplaying factor of the game, you can join well known and approved societies such as the Benedictine Order, or some which are a bit more controversial for the religious period such as the scientific Hermetic Society or something very dark and unorthodox, such as Lucifer's Own where you worship the devil. All socities that get added to the game add new unique events and powers to your character, someone in lucifer's own can use his dark powers to posses a person with a demon which makes said person loyal to them for good, downside being is that a possesed person is nuts and can lead to them stabing you in your bed for funsies while laughting like maniacs or you can become a well know saint who can teach people about good virtues, removing negative traits which is pretty usefull if you want to make sure your heir is not terrible.]

5: Conclave - [This is a rather infamous DLC as in a way it makes the game harder but also easier at the same time. It drastically expands the game's court mechanics,how laws work and how voting works in your kingdome. It makes it far more interesting,complex and in-deph, it is a DLC that i think is essential but it's a DLC i recommend for you to pick up after you spent a bit of time playing without it. The game will at the start offer already a lot of things to learn, this DLC will simply make the game far more difficult for you as a newcomer but once you feel ready to learn more and pick it up and understand the new mechanics, it can actually make managing your kingdome more easier at times as instead of having 200+ people voting for a law to be passed, you only need to make sure that 50% of the 6 [or 8] people in your court vote yes, who you can also bribe for favors or ask them to vote yes and then you owe them a favor. CK2 is a game about being a medieval lord in a very detailed world. Even if you're playing as some lowly count you'll probably have several barons under you. And above you there's a duke (maybe king). There's probably someone else who is sovereign of your sovereign but you don't care about him. You also have a family, courtiers, council. Every character has relation value to every other character as well as set of traits, faith, culture, land titles, honorary titles and claims. Thus The Drama and The Intrigue are generated. You play as a duke with a couple of counties under you direct rule. You die and now play as the son of a previous ruler. But Gavelkind system of inheritance made it so that your brother got one of your counties. That brother has claim on your duke title. He also hates you because he's brave and you're craven, and maybe his tutor was someone of alien religion and he also thinks you're infidel. He will always plot against you and will start a rebellion if you're weak.

In theory that is interesting. But it requires some imagination and attention to details. You may not even notice any special behavior on behalf of said brother. You'll have to struggle through UI to see those relationships. Your brother may plot to kill you but he won't have enough accomplices to do that, and your spymaster will automatically tell him to stop. He will use generic phrases when sending you messages. He won't pay you as much taxes but it won't be that noticeable. You won't get any special events about him and you may still get generic events about him. If you send him to work as councilor he'll do his job as well as any other character. And by the way, this council jobs are the only place where character stats matter - and their influence is not that noticeable.

All the character stuff is very subtle and inconsistent. They affect AI but only slightly and it's hard to notice. If a character has many religious traits he'll be more inclined to start holy wars or purge his infidel vassals. If a character is craven then he will only try to start one sided wars. If a character is insane he'll get special events and do things that do not make sense. But more often than not you only notice it afterwards, you can't predict AI behavior, you don't play people game. And there are so many characters around they become a cast of snowflakes with very rare characters being important, those are often generated by events. You quickly stop caring about specific traits. When your son needs a wife you just see to it so that she's not imbecile or leper and that would do. When you put a council into position you care about his single stat, it's very rare that his other stats will ever affect anything. 

Another problem with complexity: the game is so granular it's hard for it to be historical. More abstracted games like Europa Universalis or even Civilization don't show you specific details so they don't show you something that is definitely wrong. Like in CK2 Kievan Rota system is not shown at all even though you have very clearly defined succession laws. Many things that happened in history are impossible in CK2 like alliances between crusaders and local Muslim rulers, settlement of Iceland, Lithuanian dukes switching religion at will, Catholic and Orthodox church officially parting ways, violent coups without civil war and so on.

Still an interesting experience, mostly as roleplaying. Be ready to fight the interface. You'll probably be better off using Bigger Interface mod if you have 1080p screen. Also Century Gothic Font mod works well. Ah, also no UI scaling so 4K doesn't work even with mods.

About DLC. In the basic game you can play as any feudal character of Christian faith (includes heresies). DLCs add support for playing as Muslim, Republic Doge, Jewish, Indian, Nomad, Pagan characters. Don't rush getting those, see if you like the base game. Many expansions work on base game mechanics, of those I recommend Conclave (makes council much more influential and interesting to deal with) and Way of Life (adds personal focuses for characters allowing for deeper roleplaying). Old Gods and Charlemagne expansions add new dates but don't rush to play those - those earlier dates don't work as well and feel odd trying to fit Dark Ages into feudal model. Some of the content is also very poorly supported, Republics have a lot of bugs associated with them, earliest start date has special events that don't work well with later mechanics.

One type of DLCs you'll probably need is portrait one. Even with those DLCs you're surrounded by clones and it's hard to immerse yourself into the game. But without those there are like 2 sets of portraits for thousands of characters.

Crusader Kings II. Crusader Kings Two. Crusader Kings The Second. So, why the hell do I have 500+ hours on this game? Well, it's incredibly fun. Crusader Kings II is a Grand Strategy Game (not like civilization, an actual grand strategy) set in the middle ages all the way to the fall of the Eastern Roman Empire. If you have no DLC, then that is 1066-1453. Already you have a whole lot of time to do a whole lot of stuff. So what is the stuff that you can do? All this time, and what to do with it? Glad you didn't ask. You play as whoever you want in any of the starts you choose. So, the main goal of Crusader Kings II is to ensure your dynasty (house, family, ect) stay alive. If you're the last of your line, and you die, well boy, game over. So you get yourself a wife and she's pregnant and all that jazz. Now what? That in my opinion is the best thing about crusader kings ii. Not getting your wife pregnant, but the ability to do a whole lot of stuff. Maybe I want to be a Conqueror. So I couuuld play as Wiliam 'The Bastard' and conquer England as he did historically.  Orr I could be an Irish count and conquer Ireland the rest of the British Isles using a complex system of Marriage, claims, and warfare. Did I mention intrigue? Oh yeah, let's delve into that. You want to kill some guy. You start up a plot to kill him, you have to bribe a bunch of people to get them in on it too and soon enough, you have him fall off the balcony he leans at every single day. but for some reason, you were discovered. You're now a known murderer. His family will absolutely hate you, your realm will dislike you for your actions and you may be at the risk of losing it all. The factions start filling up, bribes start to go through every duke and count in your realm and within a few years you get an ultimatum to get off your throne in exchange for this random guy. There it is, a decisive battle between your armies and the people who revolted against your truly benevelont rule (killing only one guy during your rule. truly benevolent.) anddd you lose. Sometimes, it's much more interesting when you lose. A New King, and you're just a lowly duke or count once more. That's  the fun of it, you rise, and you fall. This is by far the most accessible of the Grand Strategy Games that Paradox has made. A wonderfully convoluted game, where you define your goals and the means to achieve them. Be warned, you learn this game by playing it, gradually blooming into one of the most magnificent machiavellian meanies (darn you, profanity filter) the world has ever seen. Rewrite history as you see fit, Scheme and plot, command armies and then laugh at your demise at the hands of your subjects, your enemies, your supposed friends, your children and the wonderfully cruel winds of change and chance.

But be warned, this game does not provide you with a goal aside from survival of your dynasty. Do you wish to unite Ireland and then subjugate the heathens that currently hold Jerusalem? How about bringing forth the downfall of the Holy Roman Empire as just a lowly Count of France? Or maybe you really just want to make that one guy pay who plotted the death of your insane, crippled and infirm Court Jester? Do what you want and suffer the consequences.

All in all, this game is ripe with dark humour and seems to be easy at first. But it deceives you, sucking you in and suddenly gripping you by the balls, as you die from consumption, your son gets killed in a crusade and your remaining heir turns out to be gay, possessed and a complete lackwit, all while your allies drag you into wars and your vassals rise up in arms against you.

So, laugh at the cruel twists of fate, or grow mad from the revelation. Or maybe just enjoy a quiet, uneventful life as a lowly vassal to better lords.

Crusader kings 2 is an amazing game, but that doesn't mean you'll like it.

The good: Crusader kings is as much a story teller as it is a strategy game and the possibilities are endless. Your ruler could be incredibly pious and kind to everyone, or he could be a master seducer who leaves dozens of bastards in his wake. You could be warmongering savages bent on burning civilization to the ground, or you could build incredible centers of learning and bring in the new era centuries ahead of time. As you play, you get to know your families dynamics. You might have an erratic cousin who causes trouble, or a daughter who gets pregnant, or a son who gets killed. And how you deal with all these situations actually matters. It really has a way of making you care about the characters which just makes it all the more dramatic when they die of the plague or accidentally inherit the throne of Italy. If you don't care about the interpersonal politics, then the state politics are just as good. Dealing with insubordinate vassals, declaring wars, building up troops and crushing enemies is all very well fleshed out and dang fun to do. With so much content to play with, its damn near impossible to run out of things to do.

The bad: This game is close to 10 years old now. For its entire life it has been receiving new content updates. That by itself is great! The problem is that the devs have constantly added new mechanics on top of old mechanics. Now this isn't so much a problem for those of us who have been playing the game for years and have had time to gradually learn these new bits as they've come out. Unfortunately, for a new player, having so many things going on at once can be quite intimidating to learn. Often when trying to introduce my friends to this game, they'll lose or be unable to do something and have no idea why, usually because the answer is complex and difficult to understand at first. There is a very steep learning curve to overcome before this game can be even close to fun.

The ugly: As much as I love this game, it has a fundamental problem. As time passes in game more characters spawn in. Familys get bigger. More kingdoms form. The game gets increasingly complex.  You'll notice that after a hundred years the game will noticeably slow down, even on very high end computers. A few hundred years in and even on the max speed setting time will pass at a crawl. Now, credit where credit is due, this used to be a far far bigger problem, bordering on unplayable. The devs put a lot of work into making it better, but its still and issue. The time investment for just one game can be dozens of hours if played to completion.

The verdict: If you can get over the learning curve and you're okay with playing a bit of a slow game, then Crusader Kings has some amazing gameplay to offer.

[b]What is Crusader Kings 2?[/b]

Explaining what Crusader Kings 2 is is difficult. There are 9 "Major" DLC"s for this game, which add as much content as the base game, and drastically opens the game. So what Crusader Kings 2 is, greatly depends on which DLC"s you get. 

What this game is though at its core, is a real time strategy game set in the medieval era's, the base game is from 1066 to 1453. The DLC's The Old Gods and Charlemagne allow for a start date of 867 and 769, respectively, allowing for over 700 years of game-play through the early dark ages, all the way to the beginning of the Rennaissance period. 

You can start playing as a Duke of a few provinces, under a King. A King, or an Emperor. 

Through this time, you will be restricted by realistic "rules and laws" which governed the world at that time as you balance your lands among your vassals, and family. Keeping the Feudal system together, your people happy, and making sure vassals don't revolt, is much tougher than you'd think. 

You could start off as a King with 40 Vassals, 70 counties, and countless castles in your control, and in 200 years, find yourself owning nothing more than a half disseveled castle in a province nobody cares about, having lost your seat on the throne, to an usurping vassal who got the better of you. 

Or you could find yourself in the same situation in reverse, having bested your King on the field of battle, and taking the throne for your own. 

Holy Wars, cultural differences. Supporting, and or working against your King, or Emperor, vassalizing near by independent rulers, and sometimes, even attempting assassinations against your own family, are all things which you may need to do, to keep your next of heir securely in line for the throne, and your current holdings and estates safely in the family. 

The game revolves, not around the country, but your family. In Medieval ages, your family "house" is whats important. As your current ruler dies, you will take direct control of the next of heir of your house, and they will gain the titles which the laws of your country allow depending on succession laws. 

The politics are setup pretty realistically to how it was in those days as well. Marrying off a daughter is what made alliances, nothing else. (Not 100% accurate, but damn close enough to be considered "historical"). Succession laws of how your children are allowed to take the throne, greatly impacts your future as well. 

All in all if you love Medieval history, and want to learn more about how it worked, this game will teach you things you never knew. 

If you own Europa Universalis IV, there is a converter which you can get for Crusader Kings 2, Allowing you to convert the world exactly as it is from Crusader Kings 2, into Europa Universalis IV, allowing you to continue your reign of your Kingdom, as you move from the Medieval ages, into the age of Rennaissance and exploration.  

There is no game that has better replayability than Crusader Kings 2. I have played nearly 400 different games, and have over 1000 hours in this game. (Before I got it on steam), and not a single one of my games has been remotely close to playing out like any other.

[b]The DLC's[/b]

I know there are some upheavels about the amount of DLC's, and some people screaming bloody murder and cash grab insults. I have to beg to differ, and I'd like to explain why if you're one of those people who have been hearing this. 

This game was released in Feb, 14th of 2012. That's 4 years as of this year in 2016. In those 4 years, Paradox has released 9 "Major" DLC's, which open the game up tremendously, and add in depth mechanics, new events, and great game changes, all of which are superb. (You can tell if it's a "Major" DLC if the price is over 1.99) 

These DLC's are not "DLC's", they are the equievalant of legit expansions from back in the day, when a developer would release an expansion to a game you had to pay for, which adds just as much as the base game originally had. 

The Old Gods for instance, allows you to play as the Pagans. All with their own 100's of new events for both pagan and non pagan leaders, new mechanics for the pagans, and opens the game up tremendously in that area, as well as pushing the start date back another 200 years. 

The Republic expansoin does, well what you think. Allows you to play as a Merchant Republic, such as Venice, AND allows any leader to setup a Merchant Republic within their own country, which greatly increases gold income. Playing as a Merchant Republic is vastly different than playing as a feudal lord, and is yet again another major expansion, adding 100's of new events, entirely new different type of game-play to play around if you're playing as a Merchant Republic, etc. 

The list goes on for every single one of those 9 "Major" DLC's. None of which are a rip off in anyway for the price because of how much each add to the game as a whole.  


So what about those countless 1.99 stuff? 

This is where I can understand if people say "cash grab", however I personally would still disagree to some extent simply because being an Indie developer myself, I understand the work that does need to be put in to make it viable. Albeit it still isn't much work over all.

Crusader Kings II is, IMHO, Paradox's best game.  It's a grand strategy game that throws many of the popular complexities of the genre such as a complicated tech tree, deep strategic combat, and a rich economy and city building out the window for very simple implementations of each and replaces it all with one thing: interpersonal drama.

  It's all about what other people have that you want and what you have that other people want, and it produces epic struggles, dramatic twists of fate, and wonderful soap opera fodder.

  At the start of the game if you have a small nation, you can play it a bit like a standard 4X.  Locate a smaller neighbor with no major allies, conquer, repeat.  As your empire grows, however, you begin to need to split up your holdings among relatives and friends- a province here, a duchy there.

  And then those people begin to want things, and have armies, and begin to plan among themselves.

  And maybe you have too many children, and those who aren't getting enough of the land start to hate you.  And maybe your king dies and his underaged heir who fewer people like and nobody respects takes over under the care of one of your trusted vassels, who may even now be plotting regicide.

  When that daughter you married off a decade ago and forgot about suddenly inheriets a third of the Holy Roman Empire due to an accident of inheritance laws and a suspiciously high mortality rate among the nobility?  The knives will begin to come out before the crown has had time to settle on her brow, and damage control doesn't even begin to cover what follows.

  Play enough of this game, and familicide won't even be an interesting enough story to warrant telling your spouse about after another play session where you stayed up three hours later than you wanted it.

  Crusader Kings II is big, and imposing, and takes a long time to play, but there's pretty much nothing like it out there.  It might take a dozen hours before you really get what's going on, and I suspect most people who even try it will bounce off of it without understanding why it's such a big deal.  If it bites into you, though, your time will be repaid with an endless array of amazing stories and crazy alternate histories of Europe.

So you want to play Crusader Kings II in 2023? I’d say good luck my friend. The game is solid, intricate, and has a learning curve more curvy than a scimitar. 

It’s a complicated game where the game play is based on actual characters (kings, dukes, emperors, warlords etc) as opposed to collectively controlling nation states, Like in total war, EU4, Victoria II/III etc. 

This allows for a lot of unique gameplay mechanics and accomplishments that most other strategy map games lack. For example….. you can fuck the wife of any lord you dislike through enough planing and interactions. 

The game play is less “how do I conquer Europe” and more “how do I make my families lineage the most epic? How do I kill this disloyal duke without pissing everyone off? how do I get the pope to like me personally. How do I send an expedition into China to put my dynasty on their throne?” 

Now all of this is solid and super cool. The game also does have a wide array of “map painting” of you want to go the “lets create a single political European entity that just gets bigger” route. 

Now all of this can easily lead to an individual sinking hundreds, even thousands of hours into this game. Slowly getting better, unlocking more intricate strategies, and seeing the full extent of AI random event generation. But there’s a catch. You might have noticed this game is free. It’s a trick, the base game is free.
